newsitem.title: USA: Violence must stop, U.S. tells Israel, PLO.
newsitem.headline: Violence must stop, U.S. tells Israel, PLO.

text.p: The United States told Israel and the Palestinians on Friday that "the violence must stop" in the West Bank and Gaza as Secretary of State Warren Christopher discussed the crisis with Arab foreign ministers.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. officials were keeping up furious telephone diplomacy with the region as clashes in which more than 50 Palestinians and more than a dozen Israeli soldiers have died raged for a third day.

Christopher, who has spoken twice with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by telephone and finally contacted Palestinian President Yasser Arafat Friday, briefed President Bill Clinton, campaigning in Texas, twice on the situation.

Christopher spoke for 25-30 minutes with Arafat and also spoke twice to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who is trying to arrange a meeting between Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu which Washington is promoting.
"The United States is working very hard this morning, very intensively, to try to convince the Israelis and Palestinians to step back from the violence," Burns told reporters.

"Our message this morning to the populations in the West Bank, in Gaza, in Jerusalem and in Israel is that the violence must stop, that peace cannot be achieved in the street, it will not be won in the street," he said.
"They have to turn their attention, turn their historical enmities and arguments and issues unresolved from the peace negotiations, back to the negotiating table."
Christopher, in New York for the U.N. General Assembly session, met first with Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara and then with Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.

Burns said Christopher would probably not meet as scheduled with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, who was tied up in a U.N. Security Council debate on the crisis sparked by Israel's decision to open a tunnel near an Islamic site in Jerusalem.
Christopher expected to talk to Levy by phone, Burns said.

Burns indicated that Christopher met an uncompromising reaction from Syria's Shara, calling it a "very frank conversation" which had done nothing to revive already stalled peace talks between Israel and Syria.
"Frankly I don't have anything positive to report to you on that. I can't say that this issue was moved forward in any way as a result of these discussions," he said.
He said the U.S. aim was to convince the Israelis and Arabs that a meeting must be arranged between Netanyahu and Arafat "or between their advisers."

He declined comment on a news conference at which Netanyahu called on Arafat to stop the "incitement", but former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger said in a CNN interview that Netanyahu appeared to have taken "a very hard line".
Burns welcomed Israel's temporary closure for the Moslem and Jewish religious holidays of the controversial tunnel, saying he hoped it might "contribute to reducing the tensions that are so evident."
Diplomatic sources said Netanyahu had rebuffed an appeal by Christopher on Thursday to close the tunnel for a longer period, saying that would be giving in to violence.

Burns indicated interest in a proposal by King Hussein of Jordan to close the tunnel while a joint commission studied the issue. "It is certainly worth considering in this sense -- we'd like to see more details, we'd like to have a greater understanding of the idea behind it," he said.
He said Christopher had made no decision whether to travel to the region to try to salvage the Middle East peace process, and planned to return to Washington Friday afternoon.
Burns said the United States had not decided how to vote on any resolution emerging from the Security Council, but he made clear Washington thought the debate would achieve little.

"I must say the focus of our efforts ought to be in the region ... It's one thing to talk thousands of miles away from the events. It's quite more important, frankly, to try to use our influence where the violence is occurring," he said.
